question: What evidence is there about how clients under 40 choose a financial advisor?

claims.text: According to Cerulli (published 2025-10-29), younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages (e.g., E*TRADE, Fidelity), so financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) finds that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.

Schwab (2025Q3, period ended September 30, 2025) states that younger clients learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that being met in those channels is a reason they turn to the firm.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger traders turn to it because they recognize trading's potential to help build wealth over time and because of its platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service.
Bank of America Private Bank's study (published 2026-06-17) finds that 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

Schwab's CEO (2025Q3) stated that young new-to-firm clients (a third are Gen Zers under age 28) seek financial planning conversations, want to consolidate loans (e.g., into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt), want advice on buying a house in the future, and want to be long-term investors who need help navigating.
For the next generation choosing a wealth manager, experience and expertise sit at the top of the wish list, cited by 79% of next-generation (wealth transfer heirs) respondents.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) reports that Millennials' financial lives have been shaped by heightened student debt, pandemic-era joblessness, and higher mortgage rates that put home ownership further out of reach, leading some to delay traditional milestones such as getting married, buying a home, and having children.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that competing financial priorities (such as credit card debt, student loans, and caring for family members) materially constrain retirement saving for more than 50% of Gen X, over 75% of Millennials, and above 70% of Gen Z, versus approximately 30% of Baby Boomers.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that a distinct generational divide persists in how competing financial priorities (credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for family, time out of the workforce, financial hardship, too many monthly expenses) affect retirement savings, with Millennials noted as the most impacted generation.

A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13) reports that across all respondents (not age-specific), the top financial goals or needs for which people would seek a financial advisor's help are retirement planning and income strategies (63%), investment management and portfolio growth (53%), tax planning and optimization (29%), and estate planning and wealth transfer (26%).

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) finds that younger investors are more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, so financial advisors seeking to connect with these prospective clients must articulate benefits outside the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services.

Schwab's President and CEO (2025Q3) states that younger new-to-firm households come in wanting to consolidate loans into a Pledged Asset Line to pay off student debt and to talk about buying a house in the future, reflecting life-stage financial needs.
Schwab (2025Q3) states that one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) finds that major life events - having a child, buying a home, funding college, or managing significant financial hardship - are especially common among younger cohorts and often overlap.

Goldman Sachs Asset Management research (published 2025-10-01) shows the financial challenges affecting younger generations' (Gen Z and Millennials) ability to save include credit card debt, paying down student loans, saving for college, caring for and financially supporting family members, and time out of the workforce.

BofA Private Bank research (published 2026-06-17) finds younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) allocate more to alternative investments and crypto than older investors and believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.

A Wealthtender survey (published 2025-08-13) found that nearly half of survey participants (48%) said pricing and overall anticipated costs are among the top three factors that lead them to choose one advisor over others.
A Wealthtender study (published 2025-08-13) reports that 73% of people consider fee transparency the most important trust factor when choosing an advisor.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) reports that Millennials have better access to low-cost investing options (online brokerages, zero trading fees, index and target-date funds) than any other generation, and that younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors must articulate benefits outside of the investing realm (such as financial planning, lending, and tax services) to attract these prospective clients.
According to the 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (published 2026-06-17), 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets.

Cerulli Associates research (published 2025-10-29) finds that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.
The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study of Wealthy Americans (2026) reports that 65% of younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials) prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
A CFPB survey (period 2025) found those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%).

Cerulli Associates research (period 2025) finds younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors seeking these clients must articulate benefits outside investing (planning, lending, tax).
Charles Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study (published 2025-10-09) states wealthy next-generation (Gen X, Y, Z) households seek transparency in advisor compensation and broader life guidance beyond investment management, plus emerging investment products, when working with advisors.
Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 study reports 65% of young investors still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.
Cerulli (period 2025) reports that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control of at least part of their investing lives.
Bank of America (period 2025) reports 70% of next-gen clients seek to transfer investment assets and investment relationships to a bank in the next year.

Schwab's CEO Rick Wurster (2025Q3) states younger clients learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.
Schwab (2025Q3) states one-third of retail households who created a financial plan within the last two years are under the age of 40.
The CFPB (period 2025) reports that those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans aged 46-64 of financial information obtained from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%).
Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study reports that 65% of young investors (Gen Z and Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger clients (Gen Z investors) learn about finances primarily through social media and family, which is one reason they turn to Schwab. Why it might matter: Schwab's CEO explains that one reason these young clients turn to Schwab is because Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

Schwab (2025Q3) states that younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers. Why it might matter: the context notes that younger investors at Schwab are highly engaged in building their wealth over the long term, and that the average age of Schwab's clients continues to get younger.

The 2026 Bank of America Private Bank Study finds that 65% of young investors (Gen Z and Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor, even as 47% use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios. Why it might matter: the source states 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets, illustrating why their continued human-advisor preference is notable.

Cerulli (published 2025-10-29) finds that while older investors tend to be more advisor-reliant, younger investors prefer to retain a greater degree of control over at least part of their investing lives. Why it might matter: the context notes that $47 trillion of wealth is to be transferred intergenerationally, making younger investors' preference for control relevant to their future advisor relationships.

Cerulli (published 2026-03-25) finds that the mass-affluent segment ($100,000 to $2 million in financial assets), which is typically younger and less advised, seeks involved advisor relationships. Why it might matter: the source states this $25 trillion market, comprising 46.9 million households, will benefit providers that can best offer streamlined advisory services at scale.

Bank of America Private Bank's 2026 Study of Wealthy Americans (period 2026) reports that 65% of younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials) still prefer to receive investment advice from a human advisor. Why it might matter: the context notes that 47% of young investors use AI to research companies or markets and 87% are comfortable with advisors using AI to help manage portfolios, highlighting the contrast with their continued human-advisor preference.

The CFPB (period 2025) reports that Millennials and Gen Z are more likely than older adults to act on financial information they encounter without further validation, especially from online sources; those aged 25-45 are more trusting than older Americans (aged 46-64) of financial information from generative AI tools (44% vs. 26%) and social media (44% vs. 24%). Why it might matter: the source notes that survey respondents are less comfortable acting on financial information from news outlets (47%), generative AI tools (38%), and social media (37%).

Cerulli (period 2025) finds that younger investors are typically more comfortable directing their own investing through online brokerages, meaning financial advisors looking to connect with these prospective clients must be able to articulate benefits outside of the investing realm, such as financial planning, lending, and tax services. Why it might matter: the source notes that Millennial children of wealthy clients represent a clear long-term opportunity for advisors seeking to connect with prospective clients.

Fidelity's 2025 Investor Insights Study reports that wealthy next generation households (generation X, Y, and Z) are reshaping the advisor-client relationship and, while they value advisors, seek transparency in advisor compensation, broader life guidance beyond investment management, and emerging investment products. Why it might matter: the source states the advisor-client relationship is being reshaped with a focus on holistic financial planning, life goal achievement, and non-traditional investment strategies, and that advisors must adapt to serve this generation's distinctive demands.

adjacent.differs_because: This describes the online resource younger investors use for information about investing, not the channels and sources they use to find and research a financial advisor.

adjacent.differs_because: These channels describe how all consumers (not clients under 40 specifically) plan to find a financial advisor.
